metadata.scope: e_scandinavia (351 non-867 baronies across k_denmark, k_finland, k_norway, k_sapmi, and k_sweden; excludes baronies where is_historical_at['867'] is true)
metadata.hierarchy_note: hierarchy reflects data/ck3_title_tree.json (save-derived de jure tree including x_script_* dynamic titles); downstream localisation/historicity mods should key on barony_key and join against their target landed_titles tree.

schema_notes.vanilla_ck3_name: Exact English localisation string from CK3 titles_l_english.yml.
schema_notes.modern_name: Clean modern/standard English display name of the audited settlement or holding.
schema_notes.modern_name_note: Optional administrative parent, alternate designation, or native-script qualifier; null if none.
schema_notes.hierarchy: De jure title hierarchy from data/ck3_title_tree.json (empire, kingdom, duchy, county, holding_type).
schema_notes.is_historical_at: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'}; all entries here have '867': false.
schema_notes.replacement_candidates: List of exactly 3 associated natural feature names and historical tribal/ethnonym names (>=1 tribe per barony) usable as localisation replacements.
schema_notes.name: Clean display name of the replacement candidate (Wikipedia disambiguation suffixes extracted to disambiguation_note).
schema_notes.disambiguation_note: Optional disambiguator extracted from parenthetical/comma qualifiers (e.g. 'Liao', 'Orkney', 'river'); null if none.
schema_notes.localisation_stem: Clean CK3-ready toponym stem stripped of redundant generic English feature suffixes/prefixes ('River', 'Mount', 'Lake', 'people', etc.) while preserving meaningful compounds.
schema_notes.attestation_basis: Historicity classification distinguishing genuinely pre-867/pre-literate entities from medieval post-867 ethnogeneses: attested_pre_867 | indigenous_pre_literate | attested_867_to_1066 | attested_1066_to_1178.
schema_notes.valid_for_bookmarks: Bookmark-keyed booleans {'867', '1066', '1178'} indicating whether the replacement candidate is historically non-anachronistic for that bookmark (true for both attested_pre_867 and indigenous_pre_literate; bookmark-gated for attested_867_to_1066 and attested_1066_to_1178).
schema_notes.candidates_with_multilingual_variants: Count of replacement candidates having more than 1 distinct language_code (ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5 or documented proto-stage code) across language_variants.
schema_notes.language_variants_policy: Include core local/classical forms plus regionally scoped vernaculars and genuinely distinct exonyms; exclude out-of-region exonym padding and redundant eng copies (eng is retained only when no non-English variant exists). Uses ISO 639-3 / ISO 639-5 language_code values plus documented Wiktionary proto/stage codes (sla-pro, gem-pro, cel-pro, cel-bry, urj-fin-pro); reconstructed proto/ancient forms carry a leading '*'.
schema_notes.language_variants: List of cultural/historical name forms: {form, native_script, language, language_code, notes}. form is always clean Latin script (or romanization) suitable for CK3 localisation; native_script holds the native non-Latin script form or null when the language natively uses Latin script.
schema_notes.relationship: Prose description of the geographical, ecological, or historical relationship between the replacement entity and the audited barony.
schema_notes.etymology_notes: Linguistic etymology, onomastic origin, or geographic/ethnographic characterization of the replacement entity (incorporating attested onomastic notes from language variants where documented).

replacement_candidates.name: Cimbri
replacement_candidates.relationship: Classical Germanic tribe attested in northern Jutland (Himmerland) south of the Limfjord.

language_variants.notes: Classical Latin ethnonym in Livy, Strabo, Pliny, and Tacitus
Reconstructed Proto-Germanic form preserved in Himmerland

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested from 113 BCE during the Cimbrian War in Roman historiography (Livy, Strabo, Pliny the Elder, Tacitus).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Classical authors place the Cimbri in northern Jutland (the Cimbric Chersonese), especially Himmerland (Old Danish Himbersysel).

replacement_candidates.name: Limfjord
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major strait immediately bordering Aalborg, connecting the North Sea and the Kattegat.

language_variants.notes: Old Norse form in Heimskringla and Knýtlinga saga
Medieval Latin form in Adam of Bremen (c. 1075 CE)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested c. 1075 CE as Limpicus sinus in Adam of Bremen's Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: First element Old Danish lim ('lime, chalk') + fjord ('inlet, sound'), referring to the chalk cliffs along the sound.

replacement_candidates.name: Himmerland
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic region surrounding Aalborg, named after the Cimbri.

language_variants.notes: Modern Danish regional name; Old Danish Himbersysel (1231 CE)
Old Norse/Old Danish stem preserving the Cimbri ethnonym

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in 1231 CE as Himbersysel in King Valdemar's Census Book (Liber Census Daniae).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Preserves the tribal name of the Cimbri (Old Danish *Himber), combined with -sysel ('district') and later -land.

replacement_candidates.name: Teutons
replacement_candidates.relationship: Classical Germanic tribe traditionally associated with northwestern Jutland (Thy) across the Limfjord.

language_variants.notes: Classical Latin ethnonym in Pomponius Mela, Pliny, and Tacitus

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested from 113 BCE in Roman accounts of the Cimbrian War and linked to Pytheas's 4th-century BCE northern voyage.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from Proto-Germanic *þeudō ('people, nation'); traditionally associated with Thy (Old Danish Thiuth) in northwestern Jutland.

replacement_candidates.name: Vendsyssel
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic region north of the Limfjord encompassing Lindholm.

language_variants.notes: Modern Danish regional name; Old Danish Wændlesysel (1231 CE)
Old Norse name for northernmost Jutland in Heimskringla

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in 1231 CE as Wændlesysel in King Valdemar's Census Book; Old Norse Vendill appears in saga tradition.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from Old Norse Vendill ('curved/winding shore' or linked to the Vandals/Wendel) + syssel ('administrative district').

replacement_candidates.name: Store Vildmose
replacement_candidates.relationship: Vast raised peat bog in Vendsyssel northwest of Lindholm.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: No pre-1700 CE written attestation verified; raised bog formed naturally in Vendsyssel since the Bronze Age.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Compound of Danish stor ('great'), vild ('wild'), and mose ('bog, marsh'), denoting the vast raised peat bog north of the Limfjord.

replacement_candidates.name: Cobandi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ptolemaic Germanic tribe placed in eastern Jutland.

language_variants.notes: Latinized form of Ptolemy's Greek Kobandoi (Κοβανδοί)
Danish rendering of the Ptolemaic tribal name

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested c. 150 CE in Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (Book II, ch. 11) among the tribes of the Cimbric Chersonese.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: A Germanic tribe placed by Ptolemy in eastern/central Jutland; etymology uncertain, possibly linked to coastal or ridge topography.

replacement_candidates.name: Gudenå
replacement_candidates.relationship: Denmark's longest river, flowing directly through Randers into the Kattegat.

language_variants.notes: Modern Danish river name; Old Danish Gudhen

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Danish sources (c. 1200 CE) as Gudhen.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Traditionally derived from Old Danish guth ('god, sacred') + å ('river'), meaning 'the sacred river', Denmark's longest watercourse.

replacement_candidates.name: Nørreå
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major eastern Jutland river joining the Gudenå just west of Randers.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: No pre-1700 CE written attestation verified; major tributary of the Gudenå in central Jutland.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Danish nørre ('northern') + å ('river'), flowing through the glacial tunnel valley between Viborg and the Gudenå.

replacement_candidates.name: Chali
replacement_candidates.relationship: Ptolemaic Germanic tribe located in eastern Jutland.

language_variants.notes: Latinized form of Ptolemy's Greek Khaloi (Χάλοι)
Danish rendering of the Ptolemaic tribal name

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested c. 150 CE in Claudius Ptolemy's Geography (Book II, ch. 11) in Jutland.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Recorded by Ptolemy as inhabiting the eastern Cimbric Chersonese (Jutland); sometimes connected with later Hallin or eastern Jutland groups.

replacement_candidates.name: Brabrand Sø
replacement_candidates.relationship: Glacial valley lake immediately west of Aarhus.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: No pre-1700 CE written attestation verified; glacial valley lake just west of Aarhus.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the adjacent Brabrand parish (Old Danish *Brabrand, 'broad clearing by fire') + sø ('lake').

replacement_candidates.name: Kalø Vig
replacement_candidates.relationship: Bay opening off the eastern Jutland coast northeast of Aarhus.

language_variants.notes: Modern Danish bay name; island attested as Kalvø in 1313 CE

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Island of Kalø attested in 1313 CE (Kalvø) when King Erik Menved built Kalø Castle.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Danish kalv ('calf') + ø ('island') + vig ('bay, cove'), referring to the bay sheltering Kalø.

replacement_candidates.name: Jutes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Early medieval Germanic people inhabiting the Jutland peninsula.

language_variants.notes: Early medieval Latin form in Bede (731 CE); also Eutii in Venantius Fortunatus
Old Norse ethnonym for the inhabitants of Jutland

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Earliest classical precursor Eudoses attested in Tacitus's Germania (98 CE); Eutii/Iutae attested from c. 580 CE and 731 CE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Eutōz, giving rise to Old Norse Jótar and Jutland (Jylland); closely linked to Tacitus's Eudoses.

replacement_candidates.name: Ejer Bavnehøj
replacement_candidates.relationship: Prominent moraine hill summit in eastern Jutland north of Jelling.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: No pre-1700 CE written attestation verified; highest natural ridge summit in Jutland's eastern moraine hills.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Compound of Ejer (local village/ridge name) and bavnehøj ('beacon hill', from Old Danish *bakn 'beacon' + høj 'hill').

replacement_candidates.name: Vejle Fjord
replacement_candidates.relationship: Deep glacial fjord on the eastern Jutland coast just east of Jelling.

language_variants.notes: Modern Danish fjord name; Old Danish Wæthel ('ford') attested 1256 CE

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: The associated ford/settlement name Wæthel is attested in 1256 CE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Danish wæthel ('ford, shallow crossing') + fjord ('inlet'), denoting the deep glacial inlet of eastern Jutland.

replacement_candidates.name: Charudes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Classical Germanic tribe of Jutland.

language_variants.notes: Classical Latin form in Julius Caesar (Commentarii de Bello Gallico); Charudes in Ptolemy

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 58 BCE (Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.31, as Harudes; later 14 CE in Augustus's Res Gestae as Charydes).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *haruþaz ('forest, woodland'); their Jutlandic homeland survives in Hardsyssel (Old Danish Harthæsysæl).

replacement_candidates.name: Kalø Vig
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major bay on the southern coast of the Djursland peninsula.

language_variants.notes: Modern Danish bay name; island attested as Kalvø in 1313 CE

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Island of Kalø attested in 1313 CE (Kalvø) when King Erik Menved built Kalø Castle.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Danish kalv ('calf') + ø ('island') + vig ('bay, cove'), referring to the bay sheltering Kalø.

replacement_candidates.name: Kattegat
replacement_candidates.relationship: Sea bordering the Djursland peninsula to the north and east.

language_variants.notes: Old Norse name ('Jutland Sea') used in medieval sagas

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Kattegat attested from c. 1600 CE in Dutch/Scandinavian maritime charts; medieval Norse sources call it Jótlandshaf.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Dutch Kattegat ('cat's hole'), sailors' slang for the narrow, treacherous straits between Jutland and Sweden/Zealand.

replacement_candidates.name: Charudes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Classical Germanic tribe whose name survives in western Jutland's Hardsyssel.

language_variants.notes: Classical Latin form in Julius Caesar (Commentarii de Bello Gallico); Charudes in Ptolemy

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 58 BCE (Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.31, as Harudes; later 14 CE in Augustus's Res Gestae as Charydes).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *haruþaz ('forest, woodland'); their Jutlandic homeland survives in Hardsyssel (Old Danish Harthæsysæl).

replacement_candidates.name: Skjern River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Denmark's most water-rich river, emptying just south of Ringkøbing.

language_variants.notes: Modern Danish river name; Old Danish Skern

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Skjern is attested in medieval Danish records by 1340 CE.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Derived from Old Danish *skærn ('clear, bright' or 'mud/mire') + å ('river'), Denmark's most water-rich river.

replacement_candidates.name: Stadil Fjord
replacement_candidates.relationship: Coastal lagoon immediately north of Ringkøbing.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: No pre-1700 CE written attestation verified; brackish coastal lagoon in western Jutland.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Stadil parish (Old Danish *Stathæl) + fjord, denoting the shallow coastal lake north of Ringkøbing.

replacement_candidates.name: Jutes

replacement_candidates.name: Storå

replacement_candidates.name: Nissum Fjord
replacement_candidates.relationship: Coastal lagoon at the mouth of the Storå west of Holstebro.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: No pre-1700 CE written attestation verified; shallow coastal lagoon in western Jutland.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Nørre Nissum (Old Danish *Næsnæs / *Nisum) + fjord, separated from the North Sea by Bøvling Klit.

replacement_candidates.name: Teutons

replacement_candidates.name: Salling

replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Likely from an old topographic root *sal- ('dark/grey' or 'willow') with the suffix -ing, denoting the peninsula in the Limfjord.

replacement_candidates.name: Karup River

replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Karup (Old Danish *Karthorp) + å ('river'), draining the central Jutlandic heathland.

replacement_candidates.name: Rold Skov

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: No pre-1700 CE written attestation verified; one of Denmark's largest ancient woodlands.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Rold village (Old Danish *Rold, 'hillside/ridge') + skov ('forest'), spanning the hills of Himmerland.

replacement_candidates.name: Danes

replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Commonly derived from Proto-Germanic *daniz ('lowland, flatland') or Old English denu ('valley'), referring to the flatlands of southern Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Funen

replacement_candidates.name: Kerteminde Fjord

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Bergen charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Literally 'town fjord', from by ('town') and fjörðr ('fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Ulriken
replacement_candidates.relationship: Highest of the Seven Mountains rising directly east of Bergen.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1200 CE (Old Norse sagas and medieval Bergen records as Alrekr).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Alrekr ('the towering one'), later corrupted to Ulriken.

replacement_candidates.name: Charudes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of Hordaland inhabiting the Bergen fjord basin.

language_variants.notes: 1st-century BCE Latin form in Julius Caesar

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 58 BCE (Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.31, as Harudes; later 14 CE in Augustus's Res Gestae as Charydes).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Haruðōz ('forest-dwellers'), cognate with Old Norse Hörðar, who gave their name to Hordaland.

replacement_candidates.name: Osterfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Long fjord in Nordhordland north of Bergen.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Hordaland charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Osterøy (Old Norse Ostr) plus fjörðr.

replacement_candidates.name: Fensfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Fjord forming the northern boundary of Nordhordland toward Sogn.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Hordaland and Sogn diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse fen ('marsh, fen') or an old fjord name *Fenis plus fjörðr.

replacement_candidates.name: Charudes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of Nordhordland.

language_variants.notes: 1st-century BCE Latin form in Julius Caesar

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 58 BCE (Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.31, as Harudes; later 14 CE in Augustus's Res Gestae as Charydes).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Haruðōz ('forest-dwellers'), cognate with Old Norse Hörðar, who gave their name to Hordaland.

replacement_candidates.name: Bømlafjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Outer section of the Hardangerfjord in Sunnhordland.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Sunnhordland charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the island Bømlo (Old Norse *Bymla) plus fjörðr.

replacement_candidates.name: Etnefjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Fjord in southern Sunnhordland extending inland to Etne.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Sunnhordland diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the river Etne (Old Norse Etna, 'the eating/eroding one').

replacement_candidates.name: Charudes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of Sunnhordland.

language_variants.notes: 1st-century BCE Latin form in Julius Caesar

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 58 BCE (Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.31, as Harudes; later 14 CE in Augustus's Res Gestae as Charydes).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Haruðōz ('forest-dwellers'), cognate with Old Norse Hörðar, who gave their name to Hordaland.

replacement_candidates.name: Sørfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: 38-km-long southern branch of the Hardangerfjord.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Hardanger charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Literally 'south fjord', from Old Norse suðr ('south') and fjörðr ('fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Folgefonna
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large plateau glacier on the Folgefonn peninsula in Hardanger.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1500 CE (early modern Hardanger records).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Compound of folga ('thin snow cover') and fonn ('snowfield, glacier').

replacement_candidates.name: Charudes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of Hordaland and Hardanger.

language_variants.notes: 1st-century BCE Latin form in Julius Caesar

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 58 BCE (Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.31, as Harudes; later 14 CE in Augustus's Res Gestae as Charydes).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Haruðōz ('forest-dwellers'), cognate with Old Norse Hörðar, who gave their name to Hordaland.

replacement_candidates.name: Vangsvatnet
replacement_candidates.relationship: Central lake of the Voss valley at Vossevangen.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Voss diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Compound of vangr ('meadow, open field') and vatn ('lake').

replacement_candidates.name: Bolstadfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Fjord at the western outlet of the Voss river system.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Hordaland charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Compound of bólstaðr ('homestead, farm') and fjörðr ('fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Charudes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of interior Hordaland around Voss.

language_variants.notes: 1st-century BCE Latin form in Julius Caesar

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 58 BCE (Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.31, as Harudes; later 14 CE in Augustus's Res Gestae as Charydes).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Haruðōz ('forest-dwellers'), cognate with Old Norse Hörðar, who gave their name to Hordaland.

replacement_candidates.name: Hafrsfjord
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historic fjord on the northern edge of Jæren.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 900 CE (Þorbjörn Hornklofi's Haraldskvæði, commemorating the Battle of Hafrsfjord).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Compound of hafr ('he-goat', or an old word for rock/crag) and fjörðr ('fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Figgjoelva
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal river crossing the Jæren coastal plain.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Rogaland diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Figgja, of uncertain pre-Norse or Proto-Germanic origin.

replacement_candidates.name: Rugii
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of Rogaland inhabiting the Jæren plain.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: First recorded by Tacitus (98 CE); their 5th-century kingdom (Rugiland) north of the Danube is documented in Eugippius's Vita Sancti Severini (511 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Rugīz ('rye-eaters' or 'rye-growers'), cognate with Old Norse Rygir, who gave their name to Rogaland.

replacement_candidates.name: Boknafjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Vast fjord system dominating Rogaland and Ryfylke.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1200 CE (Heimskringla and Old Norse sagas as Bókn).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the island Bokn (Old Norse Bókn, 'beacon').

replacement_candidates.name: Lysefjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: 42-km-long granite-walled fjord in Ryfylke.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Rogaland charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse lýsa ('light, bright'), referring to the light-colored granite cliffs.

replacement_candidates.name: Rugii
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of Rogaland who gave their name to Ryfylke.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: First recorded by Tacitus (98 CE); their 5th-century kingdom (Rugiland) north of the Danube is documented in Eugippius's Vita Sancti Severini (511 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Rugīz ('rye-eaters' or 'rye-growers'), cognate with Old Norse Rygir, who gave their name to Rogaland.

replacement_candidates.name: Karmsundet
replacement_candidates.relationship: Strategic strait separating Karmøy from the Haugalandet mainland.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1200 CE (Heimskringla and Old Norse sagas as Karmtsund).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the island Karmøy (Old Norse Körmt, 'shelter, screen') plus sund ('strait').

replacement_candidates.name: Karmøy
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large coastal island in northern Rogaland guarding Karmsundet.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1000 CE (skaldic poetry and Heimskringla as Körmt).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Körmt, meaning 'that which shelters/screens' the mainland coast.

replacement_candidates.name: Rugii
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of northern Rogaland and Karmsundet.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: First recorded by Tacitus (98 CE); their 5th-century kingdom (Rugiland) north of the Danube is documented in Eugippius's Vita Sancti Severini (511 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Rugīz ('rye-eaters' or 'rye-growers'), cognate with Old Norse Rygir, who gave their name to Rogaland.

replacement_candidates.name: Sognefjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Norway's longest and deepest fjord, forming the spine of Sogn.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1170 CE (Historia Norwegiae and Heimskringla as Sogn).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Sogn, derived from súga ('to suck'), referring to the strong tidal currents at the fjord's mouth.

replacement_candidates.name: Lustrafjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Innermost northeastern arm of the Sognefjord.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Sogn charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Luster (Old Norse Lústr, 'bright, shining').

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic population of Sogn in western Norway.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Finnafjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Narrow southern arm of the Sognefjord bordering Stølsheimen.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Sogn land records).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the river Finna plus fjörðr ('fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Nærøyfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Dramatic branch of the Sognefjord bordering the eastern edge of Stølsheimen.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval West Norwegian fjord name in Sogn charters.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Traditionally linked to the Norse deity Njörðr + ey ('island') + fjǫrðr ('fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Charudes
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of the upland borderlands between Hordaland and Sogn.

language_variants.notes: 1st-century BCE Latin form in Julius Caesar

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 58 BCE (Julius Caesar, Commentarii de Bello Gallico 1.31, as Harudes; later 14 CE in Augustus's Res Gestae as Charydes).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Haruðōz ('forest-dwellers'), cognate with Old Norse Hörðar, who gave their name to Hordaland.

replacement_candidates.name: Norddalsfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Fjord in Sunnfjord immediately south of Bremanger.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1400 CE (medieval Sunnfjord charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Literally 'north valley fjord', from norðr, dalr, and fjörðr.

replacement_candidates.name: Alden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Prominent steep-sided island off the Sunnfjord coast.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Sunnfjord diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Possibly from Old Norse alda ('wave, ridge') or an ancient island name.

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic coastal population of outer Sunnfjord and Bremanger.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Dalsfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major fjord in Sunnfjord on whose southern shore Dale in Fjaler sits.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval West Norwegian fjord name in Sunnfjord.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse dalr ('valley') + fjǫrðr ('fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Gaula
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary river of Sunnfjord emptying directly into Dalsfjorden just east of Dale.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Traditional Sunnfjord river name.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse *Gaul, related to gaula ('to roar, bellow'), referring to its waterfalls.

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic population of Sunnfjord around Dale.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Fjærlandsfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Branch of the Sognefjord extending directly up to Fjærland.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Medieval West Norwegian fjord name recorded in Sogn charters.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Old Norse Fjarland ('shore-land' or 'ebb-tide land') + fjǫrðr ('fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Jostedalsbreen
replacement_candidates.relationship: Largest glacier massif in continental Europe, whose outlet glaciers descend directly into Fjærland.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1600 CE (early modern Sogn and Nordfjord records).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Jostedalen + Norwegian bre ('glacier, icefield', Old Norse breði).

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic population of Sogn along the inner fjords.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Göta älv
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river flowing past Bohus Fortress (Bagahus) into the Kattegat.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1200 CE (Heimskringla and Old Norse sagas as Gautelfr).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Gautelfr ('river of the Geats/Gautar').

replacement_candidates.name: Nordre älv
replacement_candidates.relationship: Northern distributary of the Göta älv flowing directly past Bohus Fortress and Kongahälla.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1200 CE (Heimskringla and medieval Norwegian–Swedish border charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Literally 'the northern river', distinguishing the northern branch around Hisingen.

replacement_candidates.name: Geats
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic tribe of Västergötland along the Göta älv border with Ranrike.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Goutai (Γοῦται) by Ptolemy in Geography (c. 150 CE), and later by Jordanes (551 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Gautōz ('those who pour/men of the river'), cognate with Old Norse Gautar.

replacement_candidates.name: Åbyfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Narrow fjord in Bohuslän north of Gullmarn.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1400 CE (medieval Bohuslän charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Åby ('river-farm') plus fjord.

replacement_candidates.name: Gullmarn
replacement_candidates.relationship: Deep threshold fjord in central Bohuslän northwest of Uddevalla.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Bohuslän diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Probably from Old Norse gull ('gold') and marr ('sea, bay').

replacement_candidates.name: Geats
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic tribe bordering Ranrike and central Bohuslän.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Goutai (Γοῦται) by Ptolemy in Geography (c. 150 CE), and later by Jordanes (551 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Gautōz ('those who pour/men of the river'), cognate with Old Norse Gautar.

replacement_candidates.name: Skiensvassdraget
replacement_candidates.relationship: Third-largest watershed in Norway, draining Telemark into the Langesundsfjord.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Grenland and Telemark charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Skien (Old Norse Skiða, 'plank, cleft') plus vassdrag ('watercourse').

replacement_candidates.name: Norsjø
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large lake in central Telemark connecting the interior valleys to Skien.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Telemark diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse nór ('narrow sound/lake') and sjór ('lake').

replacement_candidates.name: Teler
replacement_candidates.relationship: Indigenous Germanic tribe of Telemark.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1170 CE (Historia Norwegiae and Icelandic sagas, as Þelir).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Þelir, inhabitants of Þelamǫrk (Telemark), likely related to *þelō ('cultivated ground' or 'plank/floor').

replacement_candidates.name: Tinnåa
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river flowing from Tinnsjå through Heddal into Heddalsvatnet.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Telemark charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Tinna, probably related to tinn ('flint, bright') or *tind ('peak').

replacement_candidates.name: Tinnsjå
replacement_candidates.relationship: Third-deepest lake in Norway, located in upper Telemark north of Heddal.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Telemark diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Compound of the river/district name Tinn and sjór ('lake').

replacement_candidates.name: Grener
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of Grenland and eastern Telemark.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 551 CE (Jordanes, Getica III.23, as Grannii).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Grenir, inhabitants of Grenland, related to Old Norse grǫn ('spruce') or *grannō ('edge, border').

replacement_candidates.name: Numedalslågen
replacement_candidates.relationship: One of Norway's longest rivers, flowing through Numedal to Larvik.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1200 CE (Old Norse sagas as Lögr / Naumudalr).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Compound of Numedal ('valley of the Nauma') and lågen (Old Norse lögr, 'river').

replacement_candidates.name: Hardangervidda
replacement_candidates.relationship: Europe's largest high mountain plateau, bordering upper Numedal to the west.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1600 CE (early modern mountain-crossing records).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Hardanger plus vidde ('wide mountain plateau').

replacement_candidates.name: Teler
replacement_candidates.relationship: Germanic tribe of Telemark and neighboring Numedal.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1170 CE (Historia Norwegiae and Icelandic sagas, as Þelir).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Þelir, inhabitants of Þelamǫrk (Telemark), likely related to *þelō ('cultivated ground' or 'plank/floor').

replacement_candidates.name: Oslofjord
replacement_candidates.relationship: Great fjord of southeastern Norway bordering Vestfold and Tønsberg.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in skaldic poetry and early Norse sagas as Fold / Vík.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Historically known as Fold ('broad expanse of water'), giving its name to Vestfold and Østfold.

replacement_candidates.name: Sandefjordsfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Fjord in Vestfold southwest of Tønsberg.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Vestfold diplomas as Sandafjörðr).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse sandr ('sand') and fjörðr ('fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic population of Vestfold and Viken.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Nøtterøy
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large island in the Vestfold archipelago south of Tønsberg.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1200 CE (Heimskringla as Njótarøy).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse njóta ('to enjoy, use') or an old name *Njót plus ey ('island').

replacement_candidates.name: Eikeren
replacement_candidates.relationship: Deep lake in Buskerud and Vestfold southwest of Drammen.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Vestfold and Eiker diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse eik ('oak'), referring to oak forests along its shores.

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic population of southern Vestfold around Kaupang/Skiringssal.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Holsfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Southeastern arm of Tyrifjorden north of Drammen.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1400 CE (medieval Buskerud land records).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Hole (Old Norse Hólar, 'hills') plus fjörðr.

replacement_candidates.name: Drammenselva
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river flowing directly through Drammen (Old Norse Drafn) into Drammensfjorden.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in medieval Norwegian sagas and charters as Drǫfn.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse drǫfn ('wave, billow, turbid water').

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic population of the Drammensfjord and lower Buskerud.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Tyrifjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Norway's fifth-largest lake, dominating the Ringerike basin.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1200 CE (Old Norse sagas as Tyrvifjörðr).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse tyrvi ('resinous pinewood') and fjörðr ('fjord, lake').

replacement_candidates.name: Randsfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Norway's fourth-largest lake, extending north from Ringerike into Hadeland.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1200 CE (Heimskringla and Old Norse sagas as Rönd).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse rönd ('rim, edge, stripe'), referring to its long, narrow shape.

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic inhabitants of coastal and fjord Norway during the Viking Age and early Middle Ages.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse norðr ('north') + maðr ('man'), meaning 'people of the north'.

replacement_candidates.name: Frysja
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing through Oslo into the Oslofjord, historically known as Frysja before Akerselva.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Pre-11th century Old Norse hydronym preserved in medieval Oslo charters.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Frysja ('the foaming, bubbling river'), cognate with Old Norse frýsa.

replacement_candidates.name: Bunnefjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Innermost southeastern arm of the Oslofjord bordering Oslo and Follo.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Oslo and Follo charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse botn ('bottom, innermost part of a fjord').

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic population of Vingulmark and the inner Oslofjord.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Iddefjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Narrow border fjord between Østfold and Bohuslän.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Borgarsyssel and Ranrike border records).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Idd (Old Norse Íð, 'eddy, whirlpool' or 'yew') plus fjörðr.

replacement_candidates.name: Haldenvassdraget
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major eastern Norwegian river and lake system emptying into Iddefjorden.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1400 CE (medieval Østfold charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Halden (Old Norse hallr, 'slope') plus vassdrag ('watercourse').

replacement_candidates.name: Geats
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic tribe bordering southeastern Østfold along the Swedish frontier.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Goutai (Γοῦται) by Ptolemy in Geography (c. 150 CE), and later by Jordanes (551 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Germanic *Gautōz ('those who pour/men of the river'), cognate with Old Norse Gautar.

replacement_candidates.name: Tunevannet
replacement_candidates.relationship: Lake on the island of Tunøya adjacent to Sarpsborg.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Borgarsyssel charters for Tune).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after Tune (Old Norse Túnir, 'enclosure, farmstead') plus vatn ('lake').

replacement_candidates.name: Vansjø
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large multi-armed lake in western Østfold.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Borgarsyssel diplomas).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Varna (district name) and sjór ('lake').

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic population of Borgarsyssel in Vingulmark.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Gjersjøen
replacement_candidates.relationship: Lake in Follo immediately north of Ski.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (medieval Follo charters).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Possibly from Old Norse *gerði ('enclosure') or geirr ('spear') plus sjór ('lake').

replacement_candidates.name: Oslofjord
replacement_candidates.relationship: Deep fjord (Fold) extending north to Vingulmǫrk and the Viken littoral.

language_variants.notes: Old Norse name of the Oslofjord

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested in skaldic poetry and early Norse sagas as Fold / Vík.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Fold ('the broad/flat water'), original name of the outer and inner Oslofjord.

replacement_candidates.name: Norsemen
replacement_candidates.relationship: North Germanic population of Follo in Vingulmark.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Nordmanni / Northmen in late 8th- and 9th-century CE European chronicles (c. 793 CE).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse Norðmenn ('north-men'), the medieval ethnonym for North Germanic-speaking peoples of Scandinavia.

replacement_candidates.name: Lule Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Jåhkåmåhkke area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1327 CE (Lule River valley attested in medieval Swedish charters; Lule Sámi siidas in 16th-century CE tax rolls)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the Lule River (Lule Sámi Julevädno), from *lulē- ("east, downriver").

replacement_candidates.name: Lule River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river system draining the Jokkmokk and Lule Lappmark region.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1327 CE (attested in medieval Swedish charters as Lula)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Lule Sámi *Julevädno*, derived from *lulē-* ("east, downriver") + *ädno* ("large river").

replacement_candidates.name: Sarektjåhkkå
replacement_candidates.relationship: Prominent massif in the western highlands of the Jokkmokk area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional Lule Sámi alpine oronym.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Lule Sámi *sárek* (of uncertain/substrate origin) + *tjåhkkå* ("peak, summit").

replacement_candidates.name: Mountain Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Tuorpon area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 890 CE (Ohthere of Hålogaland describes reindeer-herding Finnas in the Scandinavian mountains)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Refers to alpine reindeer-herding Sámi communities inhabiting the Scandinavian Mountains (Scandes).

replacement_candidates.name: Virihávrre
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large alpine lake in the Padjelanta highlands of western Tuorpon.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional Lule Sámi hydronym.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Lule Sámi *jávrre* ("lake") with a first element of substrate or old Sámi origin.

replacement_candidates.name: Sulitjelma
replacement_candidates.relationship: Glaciated border massif marking the western edge of the Tuorpon territory.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional Lule Sámi border massif.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Lule Sámi *sulis* ("island/solitary" or "threshold") + *jielmmá* ("eye/glacier").

replacement_candidates.name: Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Luokta area.

language_variants.notes: Old Norse ethnonym for the Sámi

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 98 CE (Tacitus, Germania 46, as Fenni; later c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography as Phinnoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Samic *sāmē, cognate with Finnish Häme and Proto-Baltic *žēmē ("land, earth").

replacement_candidates.name: Pite River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary river flowing through Pite Lappmark past the Luokta area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1335 CE (attested as Pitha in medieval Swedish charters)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Of disputed origin, possibly from a Sámi or Proto-Nordic river name.

replacement_candidates.name: Hornavan
replacement_candidates.relationship: Deep piedmont lake anchoring the Pite Lappmark interior.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; deepest lake in Sweden.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Swedish name from *horn* ("horn/promontory") + *avan* ("bay/lagoon").

replacement_candidates.name: Forest Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Árjepluovve area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1553 CE (Swedish Crown tax records distinguishing forest siidas from mountain siidas)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named for the boreal forest zone (vuovdi / skog) of northern Sweden and Finland.

replacement_candidates.name: Sädvvájávrre
replacement_candidates.relationship: Highland lake in the Pite River headwaters of the Arjeplog area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional Sámi lake name.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Sámi *jávrre* ("lake") with a first element meaning "calm/broad" or substrate.

replacement_candidates.name: Pieljekaise
replacement_candidates.relationship: Distinctive twin-peaked mountain south of the Arjeplog lakes.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional Sámi oronym.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Sámi *bieljij* ("ear") + *gájsse* ("sharp mountain peak"), referring to its twin-eared profile.

replacement_candidates.name: Skridfinnar
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Semisjaur area.

language_variants.notes: Late Latin form in Procopius and Jordanes

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 550 CE (Procopius, De Bellis, and Jordanes, Getica, as Scrithifinni)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Germanic compound meaning "skiing Finns (Sámi)", from Old Norse skríða ("to glide/ski") + Finnar.

replacement_candidates.name: Tjeggelvas
replacement_candidates.relationship: Long narrow lake in the Pite River valley within the Semisjaur area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional Sámi lake name.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Pite/Lule Sámi *tjieggel-* (referring to a narrow or stony stretch) + *-vas*.

replacement_candidates.name: Akkajaure
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major mountain lake in the upper Lule/Pite watershed.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional Lule Sámi lake name.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Lule Sámi *Áhká* (goddess/ancestress name) + *jávrre* ("lake").

replacement_candidates.name: Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Indigenous Finno-Ugric people of Sápmi and northern Fennoscandia.

language_variants.notes: Early medieval Latin (Procopius, Jordanes, Paul the Deacon)

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 98 CE (Tacitus, Germania 46, as Fenni; later c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography as Phinnoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Autonym *Sāmē, cognate with Finnish Häme, from a shared Uralic/Baltic root meaning 'land, territory'.

replacement_candidates.name: Skellefte River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river reaching the Gulf of Bothnia through the Sjeltie/Skellefteå territory.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1324 CE (attested in medieval Swedish records as Skelopta)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Swedish *Skælleft*, possibly linked to *skilja* ("to divide") or a Sámi/substrate hydronym.

replacement_candidates.name: Kågeälven
replacement_candidates.relationship: Coastal forest river immediately north of the Skellefte River.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1505 CE (attested as Kåge in early 16th-century CE coastal records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From *Kåge*, of uncertain Nordic or Finno-Ugric origin, + Swedish *älv* ("river").

replacement_candidates.name: Southern Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Gåaltoe area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1100 CE (Historia Norwegiae and medieval Norse sagas attesting Finnar in Jämtland and Trøndelag)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Southern Sámi åarjel ("southern") and saemie ("Sámi").

replacement_candidates.name: Vindel River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Unregulated mountain river flowing southeast through southern Lapland.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1539 CE (attested on Olaus Magnus Carta Marina; medieval coastal trade route)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Swedish *Vindil*, meaning "winding river".

replacement_candidates.name: Storvindeln
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large piedmont lake on the upper Vindel River.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional piedmont lake.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Swedish *stor* ("great") + *Vindeln* (from the Vindel River).

replacement_candidates.name: Southern Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Vualtjere area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1100 CE (Historia Norwegiae and medieval Norse sagas attesting Finnar in Jämtland and Trøndelag)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Southern Sámi åarjel ("southern") and saemie ("Sámi").

replacement_candidates.name: Ångerman River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major river system draining southern Lapland and Ångermanland.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1257 CE (Angermannaland attested in papal letters; river name from Old Norse *angr*, "fjord/bay")
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse *angr* ("narrow bay/fjord") + *maðr* ("man/inhabitant") + *älv* ("river").

replacement_candidates.name: Malgomaj
replacement_candidates.relationship: Long glacial lake in the Ångerman River valley near Vualtjere.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional Southern Sámi lake.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Adapted into Swedish from Southern Sámi *Maalhke* / *Malgomaj*.

replacement_candidates.name: Forest Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Uddjaur area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1553 CE (Swedish Crown tax records distinguishing forest siidas from mountain siidas)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named for the boreal forest zone (vuovdi / skog) of northern Sweden and Finland.

replacement_candidates.name: Aisjaure
replacement_candidates.relationship: Central lake in the Skellefte River chain adjacent to Uddjaure.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; traditional Sámi lake.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Sámi *jávrrie* ("lake") with an obscure first element.

replacement_candidates.name: Laisälven
replacement_candidates.relationship: Mountain river flowing through the western highlands of the county.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; major tributary of the Vindel River.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Sámi *Lájsso* (possibly "lazy/slow-flowing") + Swedish *älven* ("the river").

replacement_candidates.name: Southern Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Lusspie area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1100 CE (Historia Norwegiae and medieval Norse sagas attesting Finnar in Jämtland and Trøndelag)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Southern Sámi åarjel ("southern") and saemie ("Sámi").

replacement_candidates.name: Ume River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Primary river system of the Lusspie/Storuman valley.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1314 CE (attested as Uma in the Uppsala diocese tithe list)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse *Úma* ("the howling/roaring one"), referring to the river rapids.

replacement_candidates.name: Juktån
replacement_candidates.relationship: Tributary of the Ume River draining the highlands north of Lusspie.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; major northern tributary of the Ume River.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From a Sámi/substrate root *Jukt-* + Swedish *ån* ("the stream/river").

replacement_candidates.name: Kvens
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Ume area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 890 CE (Ohthere of Hålogaland in the Old English Orosius, as Cwenas)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Related to Old Norse *Kvenir* and Finnish *Kainuu*, denoting Finnic peoples around the northern Gulf of Bothnia.

replacement_candidates.name: Sävarån
replacement_candidates.relationship: Coastal river immediately northeast of the Ume River mouth.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1543 CE (Sävar attested in 16th-century CE Västerbotten tax rolls)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Swedish *sævar* (genitive of *sær*, "sea/lake") + *ån* ("river").

replacement_candidates.name: Täfteån
replacement_candidates.relationship: Small coastal river flowing into the Gulf of Bothnia east of Ume.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1539 CE (Täfteå attested in 16th-century CE coastal records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From an old coastal/Finnic root *Täfte-* + Swedish *ån* ("river").

replacement_candidates.name: Mountain Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Lais area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 890 CE (Ohthere of Hålogaland describes reindeer-herding Finnas in the Scandinavian mountains)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Refers to alpine reindeer-herding Sámi communities inhabiting the Scandinavian Mountains (Scandes).

replacement_candidates.name: Nasa Mountain
replacement_candidates.relationship: Border mountain near the headwaters of the Lais valley.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1634 CE (silver ore discovered on Nasafjället; traditional border peak)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Sámi *násá* ("nose/promontory") + Nordic *fjäll* ("mountain").

replacement_candidates.name: Storavan
replacement_candidates.relationship: Large lake on the upper Skellefte River bordering the Lais area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; large piedmont lake.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Swedish *stor* ("great") + *avan* ("bay/lake expansion").

replacement_candidates.name: Mountain Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Aviovara area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 890 CE (Ohthere of Hålogaland describes reindeer-herding Finnas in the Scandinavian mountains)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Refers to alpine reindeer-herding Sámi communities inhabiting the Scandinavian Mountains (Scandes).

replacement_candidates.name: Finnmarksvidda
replacement_candidates.relationship: Vast tundra plateau encompassing the Aviovara siida.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 890 CE (Finna land / Finnmark described in Ohthere of Hålogaland)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse *Finnmǫrk* ("land of the Finnar/Sámi") + Norwegian *vidda* ("mountain plateau").

replacement_candidates.name: Alta River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major Arctic river flowing north from the Aviovara plateau.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1520 CE (Alten/Alta attested in early 16th-century CE Dano-Norwegian tax rolls)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Northern Sámi *Áltá* / Kven *Alattio*, possibly from Old Norse *alpt* ("swan").

replacement_candidates.name: Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Guovdageaidnu area.

language_variants.notes: Old Norse ethnonym for the Sámi

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 98 CE (Tacitus, Germania 46, as Fenni; later c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography as Phinnoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Samic *sāmē, cognate with Finnish Häme and Proto-Baltic *žēmē ("land, earth").

replacement_candidates.name: Reisaelva
replacement_candidates.relationship: River draining the plateau west of Guovdageaidnu into Reisafjorden.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1567 CE (Reisa attested in 16th-century CE Norwegian tax records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse *reisa* ("to rise") or Finnic/Sámi *ráisi* + Norwegian *elva* ("the river").

replacement_candidates.name: Halti
replacement_candidates.relationship: Sacred border mountain southwest of the Guovdageaidnu highlands.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; highest peak in Finland.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Northern Sámi *háldi* ("tutelary spirit / guardian of a place").

replacement_candidates.name: Mountain Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Iešjávri area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 890 CE (Ohthere of Hålogaland describes reindeer-herding Finnas in the Scandinavian mountains)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Refers to alpine reindeer-herding Sámi communities inhabiting the Scandinavian Mountains (Scandes).

replacement_candidates.name: Stabburselva
replacement_candidates.relationship: River flowing northeast from the Iešjávri plateau into Porsangerfjorden.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; river draining into Porsangerfjorden.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Norwegian *stabbur* ("storehouse") + *elva* ("river"); Sámi *Rávttošjohka* ("char river").

replacement_candidates.name: Porsangerfjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major Arctic fjord north of the Iešjávri plateau.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 1300 CE (attested in Old Norse sources as Porsangr)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Old Norse *pors* ("bog myrtle") + *angr* ("fjord, narrow bay").

replacement_candidates.name: Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Kárášjohka area.

language_variants.notes: Old Norse ethnonym for the Sámi

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 98 CE (Tacitus, Germania 46, as Fenni; later c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography as Phinnoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Samic *sāmē, cognate with Finnish Häme and Proto-Baltic *žēmē ("land, earth").

replacement_candidates.name: Anárjohka
replacement_candidates.relationship: Headwater river of the Tana system flowing past the Karasjohka area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; upper branch of the Tana River.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Sámi *Anár* (cognate with Inari) + *johka* ("river").

replacement_candidates.name: Iešjohka
replacement_candidates.relationship: Principal western tributary feeding the Karasjohka river system.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; major tributary of the Karasjohka.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Northern Sámi *ieš* ("self/own" or substrate) + *johka* ("river").

replacement_candidates.name: Sea Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Laggujåkka area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 890 CE (Ohthere of Hålogaland describes coastal Finnas fishing and hunting along the Arctic fjords)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Northern Sámi mearra ("sea") + sámit ("Sámi"), denoting coastal fjord-dwelling Sámi.

replacement_candidates.name: Tana River
replacement_candidates.relationship: Great Arctic river flowing past Laggujåkka into Tanafjorden.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1553 CE (attested in 16th-century CE Dano-Norwegian and Swedish tax records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Sámi *Deatnu* ("Great River"), adapted into Finnish *Teno* and Norwegian *Tana*.

replacement_candidates.name: Tanafjorden
replacement_candidates.relationship: Arctic fjord receiving the Tana River and Laggujåkka.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1553 CE (attested alongside the Tana River estuary in 16th-century CE records)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Named after the Tana River (*Deatnu*) + Norwegian *fjord*.

replacement_candidates.name: Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Ohcejohka area.

language_variants.notes: Old Norse ethnonym for the Sámi

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 98 CE (Tacitus, Germania 46, as Fenni; later c. 150 CE in Ptolemy's Geography as Phinnoi).
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Proto-Samic *sāmē, cognate with Finnish Häme and Proto-Baltic *žēmē ("land, earth").

replacement_candidates.name: Kevojoki
replacement_candidates.relationship: Deep canyon river flowing into the Utsjoki/Tana valley.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; canyon river in Utsjoki.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Northern Sámi *Geavvu*, of uncertain origin.

replacement_candidates.name: Paistunturit
replacement_candidates.relationship: Fell massif dominating the Ohcejohka/Utsjoki landscape.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; fell massif in Utsjoki.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Northern Sámi *báis* + *duoddarat* ("fells/mountains").

replacement_candidates.name: Mountain Sámi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Historical indigenous or regional people inhabiting the Rounala area.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: c. 890 CE (Ohthere of Hålogaland describes reindeer-herding Finnas in the Scandinavian mountains)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: Refers to alpine reindeer-herding Sámi communities inhabiting the Scandinavian Mountains (Scandes).

replacement_candidates.name: Könkämäeno
replacement_candidates.relationship: Border river flowing directly past the historic Rounala site.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: 1553 CE (Rounala and Könkämä valley attested in 16th-century CE Torne Lappmark rolls)
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Finnish/Meänkieli *könkämä* (meaning "waterfall/rapids" or "highland") + *eno* ("large river").

replacement_candidates.name: Kilpisjärvi
replacement_candidates.relationship: Major alpine lake at the headwaters of the Könkämäeno.
replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Unattested in pre-modern written sources; alpine lake at the tri-point.
replacement_candidates.etymology_notes: From Finnish *kilpi* ("shield") or Sámi *gilbbes* + *järvi* ("lake").

replacement_candidates.earliest_attestation_note: Attested as Goutai (Γοῦται) by Ptolemy in Geography (c. 150 CE), and later by Jordanes (551 CE).
